title: InfiMed-ORBIT: Aligning LLMs on Open-Ended Complex Tasks via Rubric-Based Incremental Training
claim: Open-ended expert dialogue can't be judged by coarse binary signals; case-specific criteria are needed to evaluate the response.
layout: Single panel; dialogue flows top-down, arrow routes right to feedback and rubric boxes
description: A single wide panel shows a medical consultation on the left. A cartoon sick patient at top left and a robot doctor at bottom left sit beside a vertical timeline arrow that points down. Chat bubbles run down the arrow. The patient's blue bubble asks about nausea, diarrhea and whether to take a herbal medicine. A green bubble asks a follow-up about diet. A blue bubble gives the patient's answer. The last green bubble reads 'Open-ended Clinical Response: xxx', with 'Open-ended' in red. An elbow arrow leaves this bubble and carries the label 'How to judge?' to the right side. There, a dashed box at top holds a thumbs-up, a thumbs-down and a grey question mark, which stand for binary feedback. Below it, a green caption reads 'from binary signals to case-specific rubrics'. A second dashed box lists rubric questions: Red Flags?, Empathy for the patient?, an ellipsis and Collect more information?. The eye goes first to the dialogue bubbles and then follows the arrow to the judging criteria.
caption: From preference labels to clinical criteria. Open-ended medical responses require more than correctness; they demand explicit clinical reasoning—recognizing risks, eliciting missing information, managing uncertainty, and safely guiding the patient. Coarse feedback hides important clinical considerations behind unclear labels, whereas rubrics explicitly state criteria, ensuring transparent and clinically useful evaluations.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has powered many recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs), especially for tasks where rewards can be computed automatically, such as code generation. However, it is less effective in open-ended medical dialogue, where feedback is ambiguous, context-dependent, and difficult to simply summarize into a single scalar signal-often requiring heavily supervised reward models and creating risks of reward hacking. Thus, we introduce ORBIT, an open-ended rubric-based incremental training framework tailored for critical medical dialogues. ORBIT integrates medical dialogue construction with dynamically generated case-conditioned rubrics that serve as adaptive guides for incremental RL. Unlike approaches that rely on external medical knowledge bases or handcrafted rules, ORBIT uses rubric-guided evaluation and can be implemented with general-purpose instruction-following LLMs, avoiding task-specific judge fine-tuning. With only 2k training samples, ORBIT raises Qwen3-4B-Instruct's HealthBench-Hard score from 7.0 to 27.5, achieving state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized open-source models while maintaining strong consultation quality as rubric coverage broadens.
